content.text:
Done. The original file was an empty 41-byte SVG with no content to improve visually, so I upgraded its structure and left the canvas blank rather than invent artwork.

**Before:**

```svg
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"/>
```

**After** (`/private/tmp/gndfv/0.svg`):

```svg
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100" role="img" aria-labelledby="svg0-title">
  <title id="svg0-title">Untitled</title>
</svg>
```

**What changed and why:**

- **Added a viewBox and explicit size.** The original had no coordinate system, so browsers rendered it at an arbitrary default and it could not scale predictably. The 100 by 100 canvas is my assumption and is easy to change.
- **Added an accessible title.** Screen readers now get a label instead of silence. The `role="img"` and `aria-labelledby` pairing is the standard pattern for inline SVG.
- **Added an XML declaration and a trailing newline.** Both are good practice for a standalone file opened by non-browser tools.

**What I could not do:**

- **Automated validation was blocked.** This session cannot approve shell commands, so xmllint and Python parsing were both denied. I checked the file by inspection instead. It is well-formed, the title id matches its reference, and there are no undeclared prefixes.
- **No drawing was added.** Nothing in the file or directory indicated what the image should depict, so adding shapes would have been a guess you would then have to remove.

If you tell me what the SVG should show, I can draw it into this skeleton.
